notes: Interim ASBO section 39 anonymity appeal; error of law and quashing are clear though final ASBO had already been made.

enrichment.short_title: Section 39 anonymity for interim ASBO against juvenile
key_facts: A 15-year-old appellant appealed by case stated after magistrates refused a section 39 order prohibiting identification following grant of an interim ASBO.
The interim ASBO was granted on documentary evidence without live evidence or findings on twelve alleged incidents of anti-social behaviour.
After the magistrates' decision, the local authority and police publicised the appellant's name and photograph in a leaflet.
A full ASBO was later made on five admitted allegations with narrower prohibitions; the parties agreed remitting the interim decision would serve no purpose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' refusal to make a section 39 anonymity order at the interim ASBO stage.
enrichment.outcome: Justices' decision quashed as involving an error of law; no remittal because a final ASBO had already been made.
enrichment.ratio: At the interim ASBO stage allegations are unproved and the interim nature of the proceedings is a weighty factor in the section 39 balancing exercise; magistrates erred by failing adequately to weigh that factor against public interest in publicity, even where publicity may assist enforcement of the interim order.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates should impose section 39 anonymity pending determination of a full ASBO
Application of Worcester Crown Court ex parte B principles to interim ASBO proceedings
Whether a norm favouring section 39 orders at the interim stage should be laid down

notes: Lord Hoffmann's preliminary issues judgment on layered professional indemnity policies and pension mis-selling notification is detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Excess layer PI insurance: circumstances notified to primary insurers
key_facts: Friends Provident sought indemnity from excess layer insurers for over £9 million paid in pension mis-selling compensation relating to London & Manchester Assurance.
LMA's 1993-94 policies were on a claims-made basis with primary cover to £1 million and excess layers above that.
LMA's letter of 28 January 1994 to Lloyd's underwriters via Bowrings referred to pensions transfers and opt-outs as matters of public record requiring investigation.
Lloyd's syndicates accepted liability but London market excess insurers declined, disputing incorporation of General Condition 2 and notice to excess layers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on construction and effect of primary and excess layer professional indemnity policies.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issues answered largely in favour of the claimant on incorporation and notice to primary insurers, but the 28 January letter did not notify the defendants; clause 5 is an innominate term whose serious breach may defeat a claim without formal acceptance of repudiation.
enrichment.ratio: General Condition 2 of the primary policy extending cover to claims arising from circumstances notified during the policy period was effectively incorporated into excess policies; notice to primary layer underwriters sufficed for that extension, but excess insurers could reject claims for serious breach of AWGS clause 5 without treating it as discharge of the whole contract.
legal_issues: Whether excess policies incorporated the primary policy circumstances-notification extension
Whether notice to primary underwriters or Bowrings satisfied notification requirements
Whether LMA's 28 January 1994 letter constituted effective notice
Nature of clause 5 as condition precedent, innominate term, or damages-only term

notes: Prison disciplinary Article 6 public hearing challenge; Campbell and Fell analysis and resource arguments are comprehensively addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 public hearing for prison disciplinary adjudication
key_facts: Prisoner Bannatyne was convicted by an independent adjudicator of assault on a prison officer and awarded 28 additional days after leaving the hearing when conviction was indicated.
The sole live issue was whether the adjudication should have been held in public under Article 6, given the general rule that prison disciplinary hearings are private.
Witnesses agreed there was a confrontation; the dispute was whether the prisoner head-butted the officer, with two officers saying yes and two inmates saying no.
About 7,000 to 8,500 cases per year are referred to independent adjudicators under the 2002 Prison (Amendment) Rules.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to quash an independent adjudicator's disciplinary conviction, pursued principally on Article 6 public hearing grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; prison disciplinary adjudications need not be held in public and Campbell and Fell remains good law on security and disproportionate burden.
enrichment.ratio: Despite Ezeh and Connors extending Article 6 to serious prison disciplinary charges, Campbell and Fell still permits private adjudications where public hearings would impose disproportionate security and resource burdens; lack of state resources cannot expand Article 6 rights beyond Convention limits.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6 requires a public hearing before an independent prison adjudicator
Whether Campbell and Fell remains good law after Ezeh and Connors
Adequacy of adjudicator's reasons and rationality of conviction on subsidiary grounds

notes: Non-domestic rating list alteration timing appeal; statutory duty, legitimate expectation, and delay analysis is thorough across three judgments.

enrichment.short_title: Non-domestic rating list effective date after 1994 regulations
key_facts: National Car Parks agreed reduced rateable values for Manchester and Kensington car parks with valuation officers in early 1994 but withdrew appeals rather than recording written agreements under regulation 11.
Alterations were made in July and August 1994 after the 1994 Amendment Regulations took effect on 9 July, backdating effective dates to 1 April 1990 instead of 1 April 1992.
Loss of transitional relief for 1990-1992 was the commercial consequence NCP sought to reverse.
The Lands Tribunal president dismissed NCP's appeals; NCP appealed on points of law only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the President of the Lands Tribunal on law only under the Lands Tribunal Act 1949.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; valuation officers were not obliged to alter lists by a particular date or with effect from 1 April 1992, and the 1994 regulations validly applied to alterations made after 9 July 1994.
enrichment.ratio: Section 41 maintenance duties do not create correlative rights to alteration at a chosen time or effective date; abandoning the regulation 11/12 procedure and relying on oral agreements cannot bind valuation officers to alter lists before regulatory change, and delay here did not amount to breach of statutory duty.
legal_issues: Whether valuation officers were under a duty to alter lists within a reasonable time after agreed values
Whether NCP had a legitimate expectation of 1 April 1992 effective dates
Whether the 1994 Amendment Regulations unlawfully applied retrospectively

notes: CPR 19.5 post-limitation party substitution after corporate assignments; Parsons v George applied straightforwardly.

enrichment.short_title: Adding assignee claimant after limitation under CPR 19.5
key_facts: Morgan Est (Scotland) Ltd issued a breach of contract claim in November 2003 but was not the original contracting party nor the current assignee of the cause of action.
Miller Civil Engineering Ltd transferred contract benefits to Miller Civil Engineering Services Ltd in October 2000; assets later passed to Morgan Est PLC via corporate reorganisations.
The application sought to add the original contractor and Morgan Est PLC as claimants and amend particulars to plead assignments after limitation had expired.
The defendant first raised the wrong claimant issue in its defence; the application followed promptly in June 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to amend claim by adding and substituting claimants after expiry of limitation, under CPR 19.5 and CPR 17.4.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; Morgan Est PLC could be substituted as third claimant and Miller Civil Engineering Ltd added as first claimant with amended particulars.
enrichment.ratio: Where proceedings were started within limitation, Morgan Est (Scotland) Ltd was named in mistake for the person holding the right to sue under the contract; substitution of Morgan Est PLC fell within CPR 19.5(3)(a), pleading assignments did not introduce a new claim under CPR 17.4(2), and justice favoured allowing amendment despite loss of limitation defence.
legal_issues: Whether wrong naming of claimant fell within CPR 19.5(3)(a) mistake provision
Whether adding Morgan Est PLC was substitution or impermissible addition
Whether pleading assignments created a new claim barred by CPR 17.4(2)

notes: Large patent and design right trial concerning conservatory systems; validity and infringement conclusions are clearly summarised at judgment end.

enrichment.short_title: Conservatory roof patent validity and design right infringement
key_facts: Ultraframe sued Eurocell for infringement of a patent and unregistered design rights in its Ultralite 500 modular conservatory roof system.
Eurocell launched the competing Pinnacle 500 system in 2002 after previously distributing Ultralite products.
Eurocell defended on non-infringement, patent invalidity for lack of novelty or obviousness, and design right unoriginality, commonplace features, must fit/must match exclusions, and non-copying.
The case involved detailed comparison of roof assemblies, panels, top caps, end caps, and U-shaped channels in the conservatory components market.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of patent infringement and validity and unregistered design right infringement claims in the Chancery Division.
enrichment.outcome: Patent held valid but not infringed; design right in the Ultralite 500 assembly and panels as a whole infringed, but not individual top caps or end caps; U-shaped channels excluded from design right protection.
enrichment.ratio: Pinnacle 500 did not fall within the patent claims but reproduced the overall assembly and panel designs substantially to Ultraframe's design right; individual component comparison may show no infringement where infringement arises at the level of the design as a whole, and must fit exclusions bar protection for U-shaped channels.
legal_issues: Construction and validity of the Ultralite 500 patent
Whether Pinnacle 500 infringed the patent
Originality and infringement of unregistered design right in assembly and components
Application of must fit and must match exclusions

notes: Important SEND section 316 and schedule 27 paragraph 8 interaction following MH; tribunal decision quashed on narrow paragraph 8 scope.

enrichment.short_title: Section 316 not applicable to schedule 27 paragraph 8 school change

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001

key_facts: Parents of a five-year-old boy with global development delay sought to substitute a mainstream primary school for a named special school in Part 4 of his statement under schedule 27 paragraph 8.
The local authority refused; the SEND tribunal allowed the appeal relying on section 316 mainstreaming duty rather than paragraph 8(2) conditions.
The statement's Part 3 provision referred to special school placement and had not been reassessed before the paragraph 8 request.
The Court of Appeal in MH v Hounslow had recently guided section 316 interaction with paragraph 3 but not paragraph 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by local education authority against SEND tribunal decision on a paragraph 8 substitution request.
enrichment.outcome: Council appeal allowed and tribunal decision quashed; section 316 does not govern paragraph 8 determinations, which are limited to changing the named school not the type of school.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 8 permits only substitution of the name of the school in Part 4, not amendment of the type of school from special to mainstream; section 316 mainstreaming duty applies at initial statementing under MH but does not trump paragraph 8(2) unsuitability and resource conditions on later substitution requests.
legal_issues: Interaction of section 316 with schedule 27 paragraph 8 as distinct from paragraph 3
Whether tribunal could change type of school from special to mainstream under paragraph 8
Whether tribunal could amend Part 3 on a paragraph 8 appeal

notes: Divisional Court upholds Billson and Dorset on section 31 proviso; linked Godmanchester and Dr Drain footpath confirmation challenges dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Highways Act section 31 proviso and dedication of footpaths
key_facts: Two judicial review claims challenged inspectors' refusal to confirm definitive map modification orders adding footpaths at Godmanchester and in Berkshire.
User for 20 years as of right was found but landowners relied on the section 31(1) proviso negating intention to dedicate.
At Godmanchester a 1990 planning letter about pedestrian trespass around Monks Pit was treated as sufficient evidence of no dedication.
In Dr Drain's case clause 17 of a 1950 tenancy agreement prohibiting creation of footpaths was relied on for part of the 20-year period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review of two Secretary of State inspectors' decisions not to confirm public footpath modification orders.
enrichment.outcome: Both claims dismissed; Billson and Dorset correctly hold overt contemporaneous acts need not be communicated to users and need only negate dedication for part of the 20-year period.
enrichment.ratio: Sufficient evidence under the section 31 proviso does not require acts to come to users' attention; negating intention to dedicate during part of the relevant 20-year period can defeat deemed dedication, and private contemporaneous acts such as planning correspondence or tenancy covenants may suffice.
legal_issues: Whether proviso evidence must be communicated or likely to come to users' attention
Whether intention not to dedicate must subsist throughout the entire 20-year period
Whether tenancy clause 17 sufficed on the facts in Dr Drain

notes: Substantive MHRT public hearing ruling is clear but proceedings involved anonymity, split public/private hearing, and sensitive patient facts.

enrichment.short_title: Mental health tribunal public hearing for restricted patient
area_of_law: Contempt of court and open justice
key_facts: Mersey Care NHS Trust challenged a mental health review tribunal decision to hold Ian Brady's statutory review hearing in public following his request.
Rule 21 presumes private MHRT hearings unless a patient requests a public hearing and the tribunal is satisfied it would not be contrary to the patient's interests.

The tribunal erred in treating Pickering v Liverpool Daily Post controls as applying equally to public hearings and underestimated limits on restricting publicity under the strict liability contempt regime.
Security, clinical confidentiality, and the patient's understanding of publicity consequences were raised but not adequately addressed in the tribunal's reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of tribunal decision to grant a public MHRT hearing, conducted partly in public and partly in private with reporting restrictions.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed and matter remitted; tribunal misdirected itself on publicity controls and failed to consider relevant security and patient-interest factors.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 21(5) applies to public hearings but effective control of publicity differs from private hearings under section 12; a tribunal granting a public hearing must correctly assess contempt protections and consider security, public order, and the patient's understanding of publicity, not only the rule 21(1) preconditions.
legal_issues: Scope of tribunal powers under rule 21(5) to restrict reporting at public hearings
Whether security and public order are relevant to rule 21 discretion
Adequacy of reasons on capacity and contrary-to-interests findings

key_facts: Applicant sought permission to appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision in an asylum case.
Counsel argued the IAT had not followed Subesh v Secretary of State and had merely substituted its own view of the facts.
A supplementary ground relied on inconsistency with a tribunal decision in a related case Y dated 8 June 2004.
Lord Justice Keene granted permission, extended time, and listed a one-day three-judge appeal with public funding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral application for permission to appeal and extension of time against an IAT decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on amended grounds including Subesh compliance and inconsistency with case Y; extension of time granted.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal is properly arguable where the IAT may have failed to apply the approach required by Subesh and merely expressed a different view of facts, and where there is arguable inconsistency with another tribunal decision.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT's approach complied with Subesh v Secretary of State
Whether the tribunal exceeded its role by reassessing facts
Whether the decision was inconsistent with tribunal decision in case Y
